theme: David spares Saul twice; Abigail’s wisdom
readingInstruction: Read 1 Samuel 24:1-26:25. David has two chances to kill Saul, and he refuses both. Notice his reasoning each time, and how he deals with the foolish Nabal in chapter 25.
settingTheScene: Saul pursues David with three thousand men. In a cave at En-gedi, Saul unknowingly enters the very cave where David and his men are hiding. In chapter 26, David finds Saul asleep in his camp. Between these two scenes comes the story of Nabal, a rich, foolish man who insults David, and Abigail, his wise wife, who prevents David from taking revenge. The three stories together form a lesson on restraint.
observation: David’s men say, “Here is the day of which the LORD said to you, Behold, I will give your enemy into your hand” (24:4).
David cuts off a corner of Saul’s robe, and his heart strikes him (24:5).
“I will not put out my hand against my lord, for he is the LORD’s anointed” (24:10).
Saul weeps and says, “You are more righteous than I, for you have repaid me good, whereas I have repaid you evil” (24:17).
Nabal’s name means “fool,” and he insults David’s men and refuses them bread (25:3-11).
Abigail brings food and says, “Let this be no cause of grief to my lord… that you have avenged yourself with your own hand” (25:31).
David says, “Blessed be the LORD… who has sent you this day to meet me! Blessed be your discretion” (25:32-33).
In chapter 26, David again spares Saul, and says, “The LORD rewards every man for his righteousness and his faithfulness” (26:23).
interpretation:
These three chapters ask what we do when we have the power to repay a wrong. David is not a weak man. He has a company of warriors. He is fleeing for his life. Saul has tried to kill him many times. When he has the chance, his men tell him that God has given his enemy into his hand. They might even say it with scriptural confidence. But David will not touch the LORD’s anointed.

His reason is not weakness. It is faith. If God has promised him the throne, God will give it in his own time. David does not need to seize it. To kill Saul would be to take for himself what God has promised to give. Instead of grasping, he waits. This is the opposite of Saul’s attitude in 1 Samuel 13.

Nabal provides a test of a different kind. David’s anger is provoked by an ordinary insult, and he sets out to wipe out Nabal’s household. Abigail, wise and quick, intervenes. She brings gifts and speaks gracefully, and she reminds David of his calling. “Let it not be a cause of grief or pangs of conscience to my lord that you have shed blood without cause.” David hears her, and he praises God. It is a healthy sign that the king can be corrected, even by a woman he has never met.

Not every enemy is a Saul. Some are just fools. And the response is different. David is stopped by Abigail’s wisdom, and later Nabal dies when the LORD strikes him.

The refrain of the section is that vengeance belongs to the LORD. “The LORD will judge between me and you,” David says to Saul. When David leaves vengeance to God, he is free from guilt. And the lesson is not passivity, but trust that God will do justice.
connection: Jesus said, “Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44), and on the cross he prayed, “Father, forgive them” (Luke 23:34). Paul says, “Repay no one evil for evil… leave it to the wrath of God” (Romans 12:17-19). Peter holds up Christ as the one who “when he was reviled, did not revile in return” (1 Peter 2:23). Abigail is a peacemaker, like those Jesus called blessed (Matthew 5:9).
application:
Name someone who has wronged you. Pray for them today, and entrust them to God.

Ask whether you are trying to take by your own hand something that God has promised to give.

Thank God for the people who have corrected you with wisdom.
prayerPrompts: Give God the desire to repay a wrong done to you.
Ask him for David’s restraint and Abigail’s wisdom.
Thank Jesus for praying for his enemies.
